newsitem.title: UK: U.K.'s gas Network Code needs changes - shippers.
newsitem.headline: U.K.'s gas Network Code needs changes - shippers.

text.p: Britain's Network Code, the rulebook which governs use of the gas pipeline system, needs modification already and does not work, shippers who use the system said on Thursday.

Although the Code only came into force in March, and was only fully implemented on September 1 when the second phase or "hard landing" started, it already needs modifying, said David Pope, vice president, marketing and supply at Enron Capital and Trade Resources (U.K.).

Pope told a conference that the Code needs changing to encourage shippers to balance inputs and offtakes without using the flexibility mechanism, the instrument set up by pipeline operator TransCo, part of British Gas Plc, to allow balancing.
He also said TransCo should provide more information about volumes of gas being carried in the pipeline system, and should make charges more predictable.
"I'm concerned about this winter," he said. "There could be some wild times in terms of prices."
"In Canada (where Pope originally comes from) we know how much gas is in the pipe, we know what the target is and we know where they're at," he said.
"But we don't know this in the U.K. The risks are huge. We can't make nomination changes within the day.
"I'd like to see increased information so you can get minute-by-minute information on how full the line is. This would have a direct impact on prices -- but they wouldn't be wild prices."
Pope said that the flexibility market, in which TransCo is the only counterparty for all shippers, was particularly opaque.
"TransCo will do whatever it wants whenever it feels like it and you won't have a clue why they've done it."
Trevor Turner, general manager of Hanson Plc's Eastern Natural Gas, was equally forthright. "The Network Code doesn't work," he said. "The data is rubbish."

"It's better than it used to be, but there are a huge number of discrepancies right across the industry. TransCo says it doesn't matter because it averages out, but that's no good if you're a small player," he added.
Turner said that under the deregulated market, Eastern was adding customers at a rate of 400 a week, 200 each in the domestic and in the industrial/commercial sectors.
